title: Concussion recovery in teens
markdown:
## In plain English
Research on adolescents recovering from sport-related concussion shows most recover within a few weeks, but a substantial minority have symptoms that last months. Early, controlled sub‑symptom aerobic exercise and targeted vestibular/cervicovestibular rehabilitation are supported by randomized trials and reviews as interventions that can speed recovery in adolescents. Pre‑existing anxiety, insomnia, and higher initial symptom burden are associated with slower recovery.

## Key findings
- Across many studies, the pooled mean time to become symptom‑free after sport‑related concussion was about 14 days; return to school typically occurred earlier (mean ~8 days) and return to sport later (mean ~20 days), though studies were highly heterogeneous [PMID 37316183](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37316183/).
- Two randomized controlled trials in adolescents found that early individually prescribed sub‑symptom aerobic exercise (compared with placebo‑like stretching) improved the likelihood of clinical recovery within weeks after concussion [PMID 30715132](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30715132/) [PMID 34600629](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34600629/).
- A systematic review concluded that individualized cervicovestibular or vestibular rehabilitation for adolescents with dizziness/vestibular symptoms can decrease time to medical clearance or return to sport versus rest or subtherapeutic interventions [PMID 37316188](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37316188/).
- Pre‑injury or concurrent mental health problems—especially anxiety—and greater initial symptom burden predict more severe symptoms and longer recovery (delayed return to school and sport) in children and adolescents [PMID 32788258](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32788258/) [PMID 37316183](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37316183/).
- Among adolescents with slow recovery, insomnia is common (62% above a clinical cutoff in one sample) and is associated with worse post‑concussion symptoms, more anxiety/depression, and more cognitive complaints (but not necessarily worse objective cognitive test performance) [PMID 30887895](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30887895/).
- Parents report that managing cognitive rest, school accommodations, and teamwork among clinicians, schools, and families are important parts of return‑to‑school processes after concussion; qualitative data highlight variability in policies and supports [PMID 34806778](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34806778/).

## How strong is the evidence?
The evidence includes large systematic reviews/meta‑analyses (278 studies pooled for time‑frame estimates) and multiple randomized controlled trials for the exercise intervention, which gives moderate-to-strong experimental support for early sub‑symptom aerobic exercise in adolescents [PMID 37316183](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37316183/) [PMID 30715132](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30715132/) [PMID 34600629](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34600629/). The systematic review of targeted treatments included 10 RCTs overall and supports vestibular/cervicovestibular rehabilitation for vestibular symptoms, but heterogeneity across studies limited pooled estimates [PMID 37316188](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37316188/). Several observational and clinic‑based cohort studies identify predictors (anxiety, insomnia, initial symptom burden), which show consistent associations but are not proof of causation [PMID 32788258](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32788258/) [PMID 30887895](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30887895/).

## Limitations and caveats
- The pooled recovery time estimates come from many observational studies with high heterogeneity and varying quality; point estimates should be interpreted cautiously [PMID 37316183](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37316183/).
- Randomized trials supporting early aerobic exercise were done in adolescent athletes presenting within 10 days of injury; applicability to non‑athletes or those seen later after injury is uncertain based on these abstracts [PMID 30715132](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30715132/) [PMID 34600629](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34600629/).
- Evidence for interventions (vestibular/cervicovestibular rehab) is promising but derived from a limited number of trials with varying designs and outcomes; systematic reviewers could not always meta‑analyse results [PMID 37316188](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37316188/).
- Observational findings linking anxiety, insomnia, and other factors to delayed recovery show associations from clinic samples and cannot by themselves prove these factors cause longer recovery; sample characteristics (e.g., tertiary clinic patients) may limit generalizability [PMID 32788258](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32788258/) [PMID 30887895](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30887895/)

## Sources
Based on 8 PubMed abstracts: 3 research articles, 2 randomized controlled trials, 1 meta-analysis, 1 systematic review, 1 narrative review. Abstracts only, not full papers. Includes pooled evidence (a meta-analysis or systematic review).

1. Clinical recovery from concussion-return to school and sport: a systematic review and meta-analysis. *British journal of sports medicine, 2023* · Meta-analysis · [PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37316183/)
2. Early Subthreshold Aerobic Exercise for Sport-Related Concussion: A Randomized Clinical Trial. *JAMA pediatrics, 2019* · Randomized controlled trial · [PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30715132/)
3. Early targeted heart rate aerobic exercise versus placebo stretching for sport-related concussion in adolescents: a randomised controlled trial. *The Lancet. Child & adolescent health, 2021* · Randomized controlled trial · [PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34600629/)
4. Targeted interventions and their effect on recovery in children, adolescents and adults who have sustained a sport-related concussion: a systematic review. *British journal of sports medicine, 2023* · Systematic review · [PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37316188/)
5. Predicting Concussion Recovery in Children and Adolescents in the Emergency Department. *Current neurology and neuroscience reports, 2018* · Narrative review · [PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30232559/)
6. Concussion Recovery in Children and Adolescents: A Qualitative Study of Parents' Experiences. *The Journal of school health, 2022* · Research article · [PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34806778/)
7. Insomnia in Adolescents with Slow Recovery from Concussion. *Journal of neurotrauma, 2019* · Research article · [PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30887895/)
8. Concussion symptomology and recovery in children and adolescents with pre-existing anxiety. *Journal of neurology, neurosurgery, and psychiatry, 2020* · Research article · [PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32788258/)
